content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli is an edible vegetable from the Brassica oleracea var. italica family. Cooked broccoli retains most of its vitamins and minerals, offering a mild flavor and tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli is sometimes called a "mini tree" because its florets resemble tiny crowns.
It was domesticated in the Mediterranean region over 2,000 years ago.
Cooking broccoli releases more vitamin C than eating it raw by breaking cell walls.
Broccoli is rich in glucosinolates, compounds linked to cancer‑protective effects.
In Japan, broccoli is often served with soy sauce and sesame oil.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: 100 g of cooked broccoli provides about 89 mg of vitamin C, supporting immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene, lutein, and zeaxanthin protect cells from oxidative stress and support eye health.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Broccoli contains raffinose, which can cause gas in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Interaction with blood thinners
items.content: High vitamin K content may reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to cruciferous vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Broccoli can be boiled, steamed, roasted, or stir‑fried. Cooked broccoli is commonly added to salads, soups, pasta, omelets, or served as a side dish. Lightly seasoning with salt, olive oil, or lemon juice enhances its flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh broccoli in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or a container with a damp paper towel – up to 5 days. Cooked broccoli should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge for no more than 3‑4 days.

cereal-or-granola-bar-oats-nuts-coated-w.title: Cereal or Granola Bar with Oats, Nuts and Non-Chocolate Coating

content.title: About
content.content: The cereal or granola bar with oats, nuts and a non‑chocolate coating is a nutritious snack made from whole oat flakes, a blend of nuts (almonds, walnuts, hazelnuts) and a light glaze without cocoa. It combines a crunchy texture, natural sweetness and a rich supply of vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown for over 10,000 years.
Nuts in the bar provide plant protein and healthy fats, contributing to long‑lasting satiety.
Non‑chocolate glaze is often made from honey, maple syrup or fruit purées, making it less calorie‑dense than traditional chocolate coating.
These bars are convenient to carry: they do not melt at room temperature and do not require refrigeration.
The combination of oats and nuts boosts both soluble and insoluble fiber content, beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Oats contain soluble beta‑glucan fiber, which helps regulate blood sugar levels and supports heart health.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Nuts supply monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both oats and nuts are sources of thiamine, niacin, folate and vitamin B6, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The bar contains magnesium, phosphorus, iron and zinc, important for muscle, nerve and immune function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Nuts provide vitamin E and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: The product may trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to nuts.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of its fat content, the bar is energy‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Gluten presence
items.content: Oats are often processed on equipment shared with wheat, so trace gluten may be present.

items.title: Sugar in glaze
items.content: Even without chocolate, the glaze may contain honey or syrup, raising the sugar level.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bar can be eaten straight as a snack, sliced into yogurt, kefir or oatmeal, or used as an energy boost before workouts or outdoor activities.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bars in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer storage (over 3 months) keep them in the refrigerator to prevent the nuts from going rancid.

content.title: About
content.content: The Reduced Sugar Cereal Bar (NFS) is a ready‑to‑eat snack made from whole grains, nuts and dried fruit, but with a lowered amount of added sugar. It is marketed as a healthier alternative to conventional sweet bars, suitable for active lifestyles and blood‑glucose control.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: NFS bars often use whole‑grain oats, which retain more fiber than refined cereals.
Sugar reduction is achieved by using natural sweeteners such as stevia or erythritol and by increasing the proportion of dried fruit.
The product can be certified gluten‑free when no wheat, barley or rye are present in the formulation.
Nuts and seeds are commonly added, providing extra healthy fats and protein.
Each bar is individually wrapped, making portion control easy.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole grains and dried fruit supply fiber that supports regular digestion and prolonged satiety.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Reduced simple sugars and the presence of slowly digestible carbs help maintain stable blood glucose levels.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: Nuts, seeds and whole grains provide essential amino acids useful for muscle recovery after exercise.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Nuts and seeds deliver monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The bar supplies vitamin E, magnesium, iron and zinc, which are important for metabolism and immune function.

items.title: Nut and seed allergies
items.content: The product may contain peanuts, almonds, sunflower seeds or other common allergens.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Despite lower sugar, the bar remains energy‑dense due to nuts and dried fruit; portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Dry fruit content
items.content: Some individuals may experience gastrointestinal discomfort from the high fructose content of dried fruit.

items.title: Sugar‑alcohol additives
items.content: If sugar alcohols are used, excessive consumption can cause bloating or gas.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bar as a standalone snack between meals, crumble it into yogurt, kefir or oatmeal, or pack it for trail meals. For a softer texture, briefly warm it in the microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal the package or transfer the bars to an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption. At temperatures above 25 °C the shelf life may shorten.

content.title: About
content.content: Tilapia is a freshwater fish from the cichlid family, widely farmed in aquaculture. Baked or broiled tilapia has a delicate, mildly sweet flavor and a flaky texture. It is commonly used in Asian, Mediterranean, and American dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tilapia is one of the fastest‑growing farmed fish, reaching market size in just 6‑8 months.
Unlike many marine species, tilapia can thrive in freshwater, simplifying its cultivation.
It has low mercury levels, making it a safe fish choice for children and pregnant women.
In the United States, tilapia ranks among the top five most consumed fish products.
Several strains exist, including “white” (lighter flesh) and “black” (richer flavor) varieties.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Tilapia provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: It contains less than 2 g of fat per 100 g, most of which are polyunsaturated.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tilapia is a good source of niacin (B3) and vitamin B12, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The fish supplies phosphorus, selenium, and potassium, which aid bone health, antioxidant defense, and fluid balance.

items.title: Low calorie count
items.content: A 100‑g serving of baked tilapia provides roughly 96 kcal, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Aquaculture water quality
items.content: Improper use of antibiotics or contaminants in farming water can affect fish safety.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including tilapia.

items.title: Omega‑6 to omega‑3 ratio
items.content: Tilapia contains more omega‑6 than omega‑3 fatty acids, so it should be balanced with other omega‑3 sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tilapia can be baked in the oven with lemon, herbs, and olive oil, or quickly pan‑seared until golden. Before cooking, rinse the fillets and pat dry with paper towels. Serve with vegetable sides, rice, or potatoes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh tilapia fillets should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C for no more than 2 days, wrapped in plastic film. Frozen fillets store up to 6 months at –18 °C. Thaw frozen fish in the fridge rather than at room temperature before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen French toast is a ready‑to‑cook product consisting of bread slices dipped in an egg‑milk mixture with sugar and spices, then quickly frozen. When heated in a toaster, oven, or microwave, they turn into golden, aromatic toast ready to serve.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The classic French toast recipe originated in France in the 19th century as a way to use stale bread.
Freezing preserves flavor and freshness for up to 12 months without added preservatives.
In the United States French toast is often served with maple syrup, berries, and butter.
For a crispier crust, bake the toast in a pre‑heated toaster oven or conventional oven.
Some manufacturers add cinnamon and vanilla to the batter for extra flavor.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Eggs in the batter provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Milk used in the mixture supplies calcium that supports bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: French toast provides B1, B2 and B6 vitamins that aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber content
items.content: When made with whole‑grain bread, the product adds dietary fiber that promotes digestion.

items.title: Low in trans‑fats
items.content: When prepared without added margarine, the toast contains no trans‑fat.

items.title: Egg or milk allergy
items.content: The product may trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to eggs or dairy.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Added sugar increases caloric density; people monitoring blood sugar should watch portion size.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Some varieties contain salt; those with hypertension should check the sodium content.

items.title: Risk of over‑eating
items.content: The pleasant taste can lead to consuming more than the recommended serving, adding extra calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Preheat a toaster, oven to 200 °C, or microwave. Place frozen slices on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper and bake 8‑10 minutes until golden. Serve with maple syrup, fresh berries, yogurt, or nut butter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen French toast in the freezer at –18 °C or lower. After opening the package, use within 3‑4 months. Do not thaw before cooking – prepare directly from frozen.
